description:
Somos uma equipe formada por estudantes interessados em tecnologia, inovação e exploração espacial. Temos conhecimentos e interesse nas áreas de programação, inteligência artificial, design, eletrônica e hardware, além de habilidades em comunicação e trabalho em equipe.

Nosso objetivo é desenvolver uma solução criativa, tecnológica e funcional para os desafios propostos pela NASA, unindo diferentes conhecimentos e ideias para construir algo que realmente faça a diferença.
summary:
Aurora is a voice-based AI assistant that protects astronauts’ sleep, mental health and performance. Before the mission, on Earth, it learns each astronaut’s personal “normal”: sleep pattern, eating habits, physical activity, emotional state and facial recognition. In space, it compares each day against that baseline using contactless sensors installed in the cabin: an ambient radar, an infrared camera and an ambient microphone. When it detects a deviation, it talks to the astronaut, asks how they feel, cross-references the data, suggests a light meal or a rest break, and requests specific tests when necessary. It then sends a dashboard and a 7-day summary to the medical team on Earth, alerting the flight surgeon immediately in critical cases.

This matters because astronauts sleep about 2 hours less than the 8 hours NASA recommends. Sleep loss reduces performance, impairs decisions and creates invisible fatigue, a factor that NASA cited in the 1997 Progress–Mir collision. Aurora spots problems early, without interrupting the crew’s routine.
details:
What it does and how it works

Aurora is a voice assistant that monitors astronauts’ sleep and emotional health without any physical contact. In the pre-mission phase on Earth, it learns each person’s routine: sleep pattern, eating habits, physical activity, emotional state and facial recognition. In space, it compares every day against that personal baseline. The device combines four elements: an ambient radar, an infrared camera, an ambient microphone and a data processing unit. The astronaut sleeps normally while the sensors in the cabin track sleep and send the data to the medical team on Earth.

When Aurora detects a deviation, it talks to the astronaut. In our example, it asks how they feel, cross-references sleep (5h23 vs. a normal 7h15), time since the last meal, pulse and temperature, and suggests a light meal and a rest break. It asks for a fingertip blood test and a saliva sample. Aurora does not run the tests itself: it requests them, records the results and sends everything to the doctors. The medical team sees a dashboard with a status level (yellow for attention, red for alert), the requested tests and the last 14 nights of sleep. In red cases, Aurora alerts the flight surgeon immediately and sends a 7-day summary.

Benefits

Early detection of sleep and stress changes, before they affect performance.

Comparison against each person’s own normal instead of a generic average.

No wearables and no routine interruptions. Tests are requested only when necessary.

The medical team on Earth gets organized, actionable information.

Intended impact

Astronauts sleep about 2 hours less than the 8 hours recommended by NASA. This reduces performance, worsens decisions and creates invisible fatigue, a factor NASA cited in the 1997 Progress–Mir collision. We want to reduce that risk and protect crew health on long missions.

Tools and technologies

Aurora uses artificial intelligence to learn each astronaut’s pattern and detect changes, sensors (radar, infrared camera and ambient microphone) for contactless monitoring, and Python for data processing.

Creative aspect

Aurora is built around “knowing your normal on Earth to protect you in space.” Instead of a generic alert system, it acts as a conversational companion that notices, asks and guides. It leaves the diagnosis to the doctors and only requests, records and forwards the exams.

Factors we considered

Crew comfort, since the monitoring is contactless.

The astronaut’s autonomy, since Aurora asks and suggests rather than imposing.

Clear limits: Aurora does not run exams or diagnose, and decisions stay with the medical team.

Scientific grounding in NASA-STD-3001, the NASA Human Research Program and studies on sleep in orbit.
